newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA's Macfarlane sees niche for cybercash.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA's Macfarlane sees niche for cybercash.

text.p: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Ian Macfarlane said on Wednesday he was sceptical about some of the wider claims concerning Internet banking and said he expected "cybercash" to remain only a niche player in banking.
"I am sceptical about these wider claims," Macfarlane told an electronic commerce conference in Sydney.

"I have no trouble seeing a time when a lot of people communicate with their banks through the Internet but I have more trouble in seeing the large scale development of cybercash as a payment medium to rival conventional cash or bank deposits," he said.
Macfarlane said he believed cybercash would be a useful addition to existing payments instruments, but would probably not become a major repository of household or business savings.

"In essence, there will always be doubts about its susceptibility to loss, fraud or financial failure, so it will be suitable for day-to-day transactions, but not as a place to hold wealth," Macfarlane said.
He said the amounts individuals would want to hold on tokens and cards would probably be small, both individually and in aggregate.
"Even though security will no doubt be greatly improved, customers will probably retain nagging doubts about some hacker emptying their accounts," he said.
"Balances are also unlikely to earn interest, and it will be easy to keep them low but replenish them from a conventional bank account when necessary," he said.

"Although some holders will be prepared to hold small claims on issuers who are not banks or other supervised financial institutions, there will probably be some reluctance to risk large amounts with companies that do not have a reputation for financial strength," Macfarlane said.

"If some new supplier seemed likely to attract a lot of funds, banks and other existing suppliers could retaliate," he said. Technology could easily be imitated, and tokens and cards issued by banks and other supervised institutions would probably have an advantage in the eyes of the public, he added.

But he said the situation was changing quickly. "It is not inconceivable that a software house or telecommunications company or some other organisation could become an issuer in a major way," he said. "In that event, the question would have to be asked whether they were accepting deposits and thus a candidate for a banking licence and supervision?"
